children: By Mackenzie Tatananni
A modest $1.4 million in quarterly revenue hardly sounds like the start of a quantum revolution. For Rigetti Computing, that is precisely the point.

"You need to be a little patient," CEO Subodh Kulkarni told Barron's ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings report. "When people jump the gun and start talking about sales growth now, I think that's a little premature."

Rigetti's latest numbers pale in comparison to the revenue posted by peers IonQ and Quantinuum last week. However, to investors fixated on the top line, Kulkarni has a blunt message: you're doing it wrong.

Rather than pure sales, "we need to focus on technical metrics because, frankly, no one's making systems that can outperform classical computers for any practical applications yet," Kulkarni said. "Sales are just for research applications."

That holds true in Rigetti's case. Management forecasts $20 million in revenue this year — a nearly threefold increase from the $7.1 million recorded in 2025. That outlook hinges on recognizing fourth-quarter revenue from a single deal with India's Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC).

As further evidenced by earnings from D-Wave Quantum on Tuesday, quarterly results can be heavily influenced by unpredictable, big-ticket sales. The $8.4 million C-DAC deal is Rigetti's largest to date, but there is no guarantee the company will strike another of that scale anytime soon.

While this dynamic may be most glaring for Rigetti given its low quarterly figures relative to peers, "we believe quantum computing is still very much in the research and development phase," Kulkarni said.

Rising revenue and early signs of adoption can reassure investors that the promise of quantum isn't merely a mirage. But developing hardware remains a long, capital-intensive grind, and the sector is broadly unprofitable. Projections valuing the market anywhere from $850 billion to trillions in the coming years are easy to dismiss as overly bullish.

Kulkarni, like most industry leaders, is eyeing a critical milestone as timelines for fault tolerance converge around the end of the decade. The term refers to a system's ability to operate accurately even when individual components fail. Theoretically, fault tolerance will enable machines large and capable enough to solve problems beyond small-scale research demonstrations.

Today's systems are far too prone to environmental disturbances, from heat to vibrations, to be truly useful. Rigetti released its Cepheus-1-108Q system in April following a three-month delay, saying it needed to refine the technology.

The "108" denotes the number of physical quantum bits, or qubits — in this case, artificial atom-like electronic circuits fabricated on silicon chips. Rigetti's focus on physical hardware stands out at a time when competitors are prioritizing logical qubits: virtual, error-corrected units created by linking clusters of physical qubits to shield information from environmental noise.
Kulkarni takes issue with that framing.

"Our view is that the industry is prematurely using the term," he said. "We don't use that word, Google doesn't use that word, Amazon doesn't use that word. The error rate for a logical qubit should be 10-10 or even better, and we're not quite there yet. While we're dealing with imperfect qubits, we should stick with physical qubits."

Rigetti's slow-and-steady posture offers a pragmatic counterweight to industry hype, even if it tests investors' patience. For now, the industry's most ambitious promises — from accelerated drug discovery to more efficient portfolio optimization — remain unfulfilled.

"We're very excited about where superconducting quantum is heading," Kulkarni said, referring to the modality pursued by Rigetti alongside giants like IBM and Google. "Fundamentally, our strengths are speed and scale."
He projects that initial commercial viability will emerge in roughly three years, followed by broader enterprise adoption over the subsequent decade.
"Data center managers will actually start using quantum computers for practical applications," Kulkarni said. "They will outperform CPUs and GPUs, and that's when sales will really take off."
